I have farmed these 14 mu in Quzhou for fifty years, and I know every ridge and furrow like the back of my hand. My wife and I are the only ones left at home now—our children work in the city—so I must plan the season so we do not work ourselves to exhaustion, but still bring in enough grain to fill our jars and sell a little. We are lucky to have our own well, but pumping water costs electricity, so I count every irrigation.

This year I will keep to the wheat-maize rotation. In autumn I will rotary till the full 14 mu and sow an improved wheat variety. I will spread about 26 kg of nitrogen per mu—half as base fertilizer, half topdressed at jointing in spring—plus 5 kg of phosphorus and 4 kg of potassium per mu to keep the soil from tiring out. Wheat needs steady water, so I will irrigate four times: right after sowing, once before the winter freeze, once at jointing, and once during grain filling. I will spray four times for weeds, insects, and the rust that sometimes blows in from the south.

As soon as the wheat is threshed in early June, I will plant hybrid maize directly into the stubble without plowing. No-tillage saves precious days before the summer drought sets in, and at my age I cannot turn the soil twice in one week. Maize needs about 18 kg of nitrogen per mu, and another 4 kg each of phosphorus and potassium. I will irrigate three times—at the big-trumpet stage, during tasseling, and at grain filling—and spray three times to keep weeds and corn borers under control. I expect about 520 kg of wheat per mu and 580 kg of maize per mu; that is steady and honest, and my wife and I can manage it between the two of us.
